folders.name: łódź, poland
folders.description:
Łódź is the third-largest city in Poland and the capital of Łódź Voivodeship, located in the central part of the country approximately 135 kilometres south-west of Warsaw. The city covers 293.25 square kilometres and sits on the watershed between the Vistula and Oder river basins. It is the largest city in central Poland and its main administrative centre.

The city first appears in written records in 1332, when the village of Łodzia was granted to the bishops of Włocławek. In 1423 King Władysław Jagiełło granted Łódź city rights, and for the next five centuries it functioned as a small agricultural and craft settlement with local significance. As late as 1810 the town had only 190 inhabitants.

The turning point came in 1820, when Stanisław Staszic helped transform the small town into a modern industrial centre. The 1816 decree by the Czar granted territory deeds to German immigrants who came to clear land and build factories and housing. Settlers arrived from southern Germany, Silesia, and Bohemia, as well as from as far as Portugal, England, France, and Ireland. The first cotton mill opened in 1825, and fourteen years later the first steam-powered factory in both Poland and Russia began operations.

The city's industrial development was driven by textile magnates such as Karol Scheibler and Ludwik Grohman. Scheibler opened a cotton spinning mill in 1855 with 5,740 spindles and a 40-horsepower steam engine. In 1921 the Scheibler and Grohman factories merged to create the largest textile plant on the European continent. The city's 19th-century architecture reflects this industrial heritage, with a characteristic blend of residential and industrial functions in the city centre and the distinctive tenement houses with dark courtyard wells.

Łódź is administratively divided into five districts: Śródmieście (the city centre, 713 hectares), Bałuty (7,851 hectares) in the north, Widzew (9,044 hectares) in the east, Górna (7,180 hectares) in the south, and Polesie (4,537 hectares) in the west. Population figures from 2022 show Bałuty as the most populous with 184,605 residents, followed by Górna with 154,064, Widzew with 132,456, Polesie with 130,102, and Śródmieście with 57,217.

In 2005 the city introduced the Municipal Information System (SIM), dividing Łódź into 56 areas for consistent street signage and wayfinding. These SIM areas are not formal administrative units but geographic and historical zones used for orientation purposes.

Łódź has experienced significant demographic decline. The population fell from over 785,000 in 2002 to approximately 655,000 in 2023, a loss of nearly 130,000 residents. This makes Łódź the fastest-depopulating city in Poland. However, an experimental GUS study in 2026 found that 698,600 people actually reside in the city, placing it fourth in Poland after Warsaw, Kraków, and Wrocław.

The city has undertaken extensive revitalisation efforts. The Nowe Centrum Łodzi programme covers a degraded area around the old Łódź Fabryczna station and EC1, with plans for over 3,500 new dwellings and 90,000 square metres of office space. The broader revitalisation programme has restored approximately 180 tenement houses, created 1,006 new dwellings, 270 service premises, and 36 art studios, along with 50 rebuilt or newly constructed street sections. Plac Wolności won first place in a competition for the best-revitalised public space in 2024. In 2024 approximately 42 million złoty was spent on revitalisation-related tasks and projects in the city centre.

folders.name: łódź, poland/centrum, łódź
folders.description:
Centrum is an area of Łódź designated in 2005 for the Municipal Information System (SIM), not a formal administrative estate but a wayfinding zone for signage and addressing. It lies within the Śródmieście district and covers most of the Katedralna administrative estate. Its boundaries are defined by the edges of Śródmieście where it meets Polesie, Bałuty, Widzew, and Górna, with Kilińskiego Street forming the eastern limit.

The built fabric is overwhelmingly historic. Almost all buildings in the Centrum unit were constructed before 1945, and two-thirds of its dwellings date from before 1918. Łódź escaped heavy wartime destruction, so the centre retains a dense mix of 19th-century tenements, factory complexes, palaces, and interwar public buildings. Post-war planning largely left the historic centre alone, focusing instead on new estates around it, and the area was only maintained or occasionally modernised.

The major post-war intervention in Centrum was the Śródmiejska Dzielnica Mieszkaniowa, known as Łódź Manhattan. Construction began in 1975 and finished in 1982, replacing a row of deteriorating early 19th-century weaver houses on Piotrkowska Street. The complex comprises eight buildings, two of which reach 78 metres and remain the tallest residential towers in the city. Nearly 2,000 flats were delivered, considered comfortable and prestigious at the time, and the towers became a landmark of PRL-era housing.

Revitalisation has since become the dominant force shaping the area. The city has run large-scale programmes targeting historic tenements, courtyards, and public spaces across the centre, with hundreds of millions of złoty invested in renovation and modernisation of the 19th-century building stock. The Nowe Centrum Łodzi programme covers roughly 100 hectares bounded by Narutowicza, Kopcińskiego, Tuwima, and Piotrkowska streets, divided into three zones: a priority area for mixed cultural, commercial, and residential functions; a zone for commercial projects integrated with revitalisation; and a zone of historic late-19th and early-20th-century urban blocks requiring intensive renewal.

folders.name: łódź, poland/centrum, łódź/central office building
folders.description:
The Central office building—the 13-story tower at Piotrkowska 165/169—is the lesser-known half of the complex that most people just call “Central.” The department store next door got all the attention, but the office block was built at the same time, in 1972, for the Społem cooperative, and for years it housed the cooperative’s Łódź administration. It was designed by Maciej Gintowt along with Ewa and Maciej Krasiński, the same team behind the Supersam in Warsaw and Spodek in Katowice, and the whole complex was selected through a SARP competition back in 1961. The tower is 45 meters tall and stands as a fairly pure piece of brutalism—washed concrete panels, repetitive horizontal window bands, a raised first floor on pillars that creates a covered passage at ground level.

While the department store kept operating and was even renovated inside in 2019, the office tower was emptied out and left to decay. It was put up for sale in 2018. A developer eventually bought it and commissioned a conversion project from architect Marcin Tomaszewski, which would have turned the upper floors into around 40 apartments, added a two-level entrance hall and service units on the ground floor, and put a gym and massage room in the basement. Building permits were secured, but the developer backed out. The building went back on the market in 2025, now with a price tag around 20 million złoty and the completed design included in the package. In the meantime, urban explorers have been inside and reported that the lower floors still hold remnants of furniture and equipment from the Społem days, while most of the upper floors have been stripped down to bare concrete. The building is not going to be demolished—heritage protections and the local zoning plan require the original structure to be kept—so whatever happens, the concrete frame is staying. It is currently still waiting for a buyer willing to actually finish the job.

folders.name: łódź, poland/nowe rokicie, łódź
folders.description:
Nowe Rokicie is an area of Łódź designated in 2005 for the Municipal Information System (SIM), not a formal administrative estate but a wayfinding zone. It lies in the Górna district and forms the north-eastern part of the Rokicie administrative estate. It was a village before incorporation, with parts annexed to Łódź in 1906 and 1915, and definitively in 1946.

Its boundaries run along Wróblewskiego Street to the north, where it meets the SIM area of Politechniczna in Polesie; Politechniki Avenue to the east, bordering Górniak; Pabianicka Street to the south, meeting Kurak; and to the west it adjoins the Rokicie and Nowe Sady SIM areas. The Jasień river flows through the area.

Before the war, the area was largely undeveloped, with brickworks and factory premises scattered among open land. The turning point came with the construction of a large public school building, designed by city architect Wacław Kowalewski, whose main works were completed in 1926. It still stands at Przyszkole Street and houses Primary School No. 42. The complex was built in the National Style, referencing Stanislavian classicism, and is entered in the register of monuments.

Large-scale housing construction began after World War II. Planning for the new estate started around 1953 with technical and economic guidelines. The layout concentrated commercial and cultural functions along a north–south axis, and the estate was intended as a model of a sunny, lively social housing district under difficult post-war conditions. The first blocks were four-storey buildings in a more economical form, and the estate was populated largely by residents displaced from demolished inner-city buildings, as well as families of ministry, militia, and military employees.

Three buildings stand out in the estate's architecture. The first is the "łamaniec" (roughly, "the zigzag"), a mixed residential and commercial building in the centre of the estate designed by engineer Edmund Orlik around 1957. Its name comes from its floor plan, where the walls meet at angles other than right angles, giving the elevations a zigzagging appearance. The ground floor has a sculptural treatment of the commercial space with a glazed display window projecting in front of the façade, and the building runs along one of the estate's two main commercial routes. The second is a health centre with a pharmacy, designed around 1960 by Jerzy Jakubczak, a simple modernist building with a functionally resolved interior and an imposing circular staircase in the main hall, referencing the latest international tendencies of the time.

The third and largest architectural event was the complex of four 13-storey towers completed around 1962, which became the estate's signature and the first complex of its kind in Łódź. They were designed at the Office of Studies and Projects for Industrial Construction in Warsaw under architect Włodzimierz Minich, on the site of five point blocks originally planned by Orlik. The towers have very simple plans and structures, well-proportioned elevations, and were built using an advanced technology for the time that allowed such tall buildings to be erected without heavy equipment. By the early 1970s, industrial building technology was used for the final blocks of the estate.

The estate has lost the flowery character it had in its early years. In recent years, the area has seen some infrastructure work, including a planned comprehensive renovation of two key streets, Piękna and Cieszkowskiego, with 370 new parking spaces, new water mains, pavements, asphalt, and trees. A developer has also proposed a new housing estate for around 2,000 people on Holownicza Street near the Jasień river, consisting of ten blocks.

folders.name: łódź, poland/nowe rokicie, łódź/EC-2 combined heat and power plant
folders.description:
EC2 is the former Łódź heat and power plant at Wróblewskiego 26, a 20-hectare complex that operated from the mid-1950s until 2015 and is now being demolished to make way for a housing estate. Unlike the Central office building, whose concrete frame is protected and waiting for a buyer, EC2 is largely coming down—though a handful of its buildings are listed as monuments, and the main hall is meant to survive.

The plant was built as Elektrociepłownia im. Włodzimierza Lenina, designed by engineer Mariusz Sowiński. Construction began in June 1954, the first boiler and turbine started up in 1957, and the full complex was finished in 1961. It was the first modern combined heat and power plant in Łódź after the war, supplying electricity, system heat to the Górna districts including Retkinia and Karolew, and process steam to nearby industry. The architecture is socialist realist, with the main building, a 300-metre machine hall, two cooling towers, and three chimneys—two at 120 metres and one at 160 metres—dominating the skyline. The site also contained air-raid shelters for several dozen people. Its industrial interiors and chimney stacks appeared in film and television, including the series Stawka większa niż życie and the music video for Taconafide’s “Tamagotchi”.

The plant was shut down on 31 March 2015 after 57 years of operation, with Veolia citing worn-out equipment, falling demand for heat and electricity, and stricter environmental rules coming into force in 2016. After closure, the site changed hands several times. A first attempt at demolition in 2019 was halted by the provincial monuments conservator because it was carried out without the required permit. The current owner, JHM Development, bought the shares of the bankrupt company Hakamore in 2021 and now holds perpetual usufruct rights to the entire 20-hectare site.

Demolition properly began around Christmas 2025, starting with the gatehouse and gate. The two cooling towers and three chimneys were also scheduled for removal, with JHM arguing that technical surveys showed advanced degradation, no realistic prospect of repair, and a risk to the surroundings. None of those elements—the towers or the chimneys—were in the monuments register, and the conservator had agreed that they should be struck from the heritage inventory. What is protected is a group of buildings: the main power plant building with the control room’s technical equipment, the administration building, the gatehouse with its drive-through gate, the social and management building, and the land itself. The perimeter fence is also in the heritage inventory.

The three chimneys — two at 120 metres and one at 160 metres—were brought down on 20 October 2026. The operation was handled by JHM Development using the explosive method: the chimneys were demolished in their above-ground and underground sections, foundations included, in a controlled blast. Preparations had been underway for weeks, with an inventory of neighbouring buildings taken before and after the works to document their condition in case of claims. Residents in the area, particularly those living opposite on Wróblewskiego and in the Nowa Przędzalnia estate, had been worried about the noise and dust, and the investor kept the exact timing quiet for safety reasons, notifying only those directly affected. Because the chimneys were never in the monuments register—the conservator had explicitly declined to list them back in 2019—no heritage permit was needed for their removal.

What remains of EC2 now is the protected group of buildings: the main power plant hall, the administration building, the gatehouse, the social and management building, and the perimeter fence. The future of the site is still not fully settled. JHM has shown visualisations of a mixed-use development—rows of multi-family housing, a shopping centre, passageways, the restored main power plant building, and the cooling towers kept as landmarks—but the company says these images, prepared for the Expo Real fair in Munich, are not binding. The current plan is described as “undefined”; JHM is talking to the city and looking for a shared concept, with concrete plans to be specified within a year or two. The scale being discussed is around 2,500 flats, plus commercial, office, and leisure space, some of it inside the listed buildings in a mixed-use formula. A new public street is also planned, linking Aleja Politechniki with Wieniawskiego, partly along the route of the old railway siding under the Jana Pawła II viaduct. Architects and local groups have argued that the main EC2 building should keep its industrial identity and take on a cultural function rather than being swallowed by housing, and residents have said the area already has too many blocks and would be better served by a park or entertainment space. For now, the chimneys are gone, the main hall is protected, and the rest of the complex is gradually disappearing.

folders.name: łódź, poland/nowe rokicie, łódź/EC-2 combined heat and power plant/boiler hall
folders.description: The boiler hall at EC-2 held nine boilers. Four of them were dismantled before the plant was shut down, leaving boilers 5 through 9 in the hall. After the site was bought, the upper floor was demolished, and boiler K-5 was partially dismantled along with it. Boilers K-6, K-7 and K-8 survived in good condition, with only the metal components cut out for scrap missing. Boiler K-9 was dismantled from the top, so it now looks as if it has been cut in half. The boiler hall is one of the best-preserved parts of the entire complex.

folders.name: łódź, poland/nowe rokicie, łódź/EC-2 combined heat and power plant/control room
folders.description: The control room at EC-2 is the only interior in the plant still listed in the heritage register. Operators worked there for decades, monitoring the boilers and turbines and making decisions that affected the city. The room had hundreds of buttons, indicators and levers. In 2023 its walls were still largely intact; since then the wall panels have been cut out for scrap. Only the main control desk survives, and it is in poor condition. The control room is one of the best records of how EC-2 operated and also one of the most heavily damaged parts of the complex.

folders.name: łódź, poland/nowe rokicie, łódź/EC-2 combined heat and power plant/turbine hall
folders.description: The turbine hall at EC-2 held seven turbosets with a combined capacity of 206 MW. That is where a significant part of Łódź’s electricity was produced. After the plant was shut down, all of the turbines and generators were cut up for scrap. What remains today are the empty foundations and the marks left by the machines. The hall is still a large, empty industrial interior, but the equipment itself is gone.
